\renewcommand{\Im}{\operatorname{Im}}
\newcommand{\bbeta}{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
\newcommand{\bgamma}{{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}}

%==================================================
\begin{document}

\title{(Strange) gamma evaluations}
% math.CA math.NT math.CO

\author{Wadim Zudilin}
\address{Department of Mathematics, IMAPP, Radboud University, PO Box 9010, 6500~GL Nij\-me\-gen, The Netherlands}
\urladdr{https://www.math.ru.nl/~wzudilin/}

\date{$1^2$ July $45^2$}
%\thanks{This draft is for internal use.}

\dedicatory{To Doron Zeilberger `The Creative' on his $3\times5^2$th birthday}

\subjclass[2020]{33F10 (primary), 33C05, 33C20, 33D15 (secondary).}
\keywords{Hypergeometric function, closed form, creative telescoping}

\begin{abstract}
We review `creative' strategies of closed-form evaluations of hypergeometric functions.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%==================================================

This exposition is a rather technical account of certain recent \emph{nice} developments in the field of `strange' or `gamma' evaluations of hypergeometric functions.
At the same time, we cover computational aspects neither deep nor systematic: the reader is invited to perform calculations alluded themself.

For details of the classical theory of hypergeometric functions and their $q$- (\emph{aka} `basic') analogues consult with \cite{Ba35,GR04,Sl66}. Examples of hypergeometric summations (and transformations)\,---\,those that happen to be gamma (but not strange) evaluations go back to at least the 18th century and are attached to the names as great as Euler and Gauss; the related binomial theorem and the Chu--Vandermonde summation are even earlier.
The adjective `strange' was coined after a list of Gosper's evaluations discussed by Gessel and Stanton at length in \cite{GS82} but, perhaps, first examples of such strange evaluations were systematically produced by Goursat in~\cite{Go81}. 

\section{Ebisu's methodology}
\label{sec1}

Some years ago, Ebisu \cite{Eb17} came up with a strategy to use contiguous relations of $_2F_1$ hypergeometric sums for proving numerous strange evaluations of the series.
Let us follow the explanation in \cite{BF22,Eb17}.

Consider a triple of hypergeometric parameters $a,b,c$ and abbreviate it by $\bbeta=(a,b,c)$;
denote
\[
F(\bbeta\mid z)={}_2F_1(a,b;c\mid z)
=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{(a)_n(b)_n}{(c)_nn!}\,z^n
\]
the Euler--Gauss hypergeometric function \cite{Ba35,Sl66}, where $(a)_n=\Gamma(a+n)/\Gamma(a)$ is Pochhammer's symbol.
Let $k,l,m$ be a fixed triple of integers abbreviated $\bgamma=(k,l,m)$, the shift vector.
Using contiguity relations we can write down explicitly rational functions $R_\bgamma(\bbeta,z)$ and $Q_\bgamma(\bbeta,z)$ in $\mathbb{Q}(a,b,c,z)$ such that
\begin{equation}
\label{basic}
F(\bbeta+\bgamma\mid z)=R_\bgamma(\bbeta,z)F(\bbeta\mid z)+Q_\bgamma(\bbeta,z)F'(\bbeta\mid z),
\end{equation}
where $F'$ is the $z$-derivative of~$F$.
In other words, very shift of the parameters of a $_2F_1$ series by integers can be efficiently written as a linear combination of the original series and its $z$-derivative with rational-function coefficients.
The underlying algorithmic strategy makes use of composition of shifts of individual parameters by~1 listed in \cite[Sect.~1.4]{Sl66}.
A quadruple $(\bbeta,z_0)=(a,b,c,z_0)$ is called \emph{admissible} with respect to $\bgamma$
if $Q_\bgamma(\bbeta+t\bgamma,z_0)=0$ for all $t\in\mathbb C$. 
Choosing an admissible quadruple $(\bbeta,z_0)$ and substituting $\bbeta+\bgamma$ for $\bbeta$ in~\eqref{basic} we obtain the functional equation
\begin{equation}\label{functional}
F(\bbeta+(t+1)\bgamma\mid z_0)=R_\bgamma(\bbeta+t\bgamma,z_0) F(\bbeta+t\bgamma\mid z_0)
\end{equation}
in parameter $t$. Viewing the coefficient $R_\bgamma(\bbeta+t\bgamma,z_0)$ as a rational function in~$t$, we factor it into linear terms:
\[
R_\bgamma(\bbeta+t\bgamma,z_0)=R_0\prod_{i=1}^r\frac{t+\alpha_i}{t+\delta_i},\quad R_0\in\mathbb C^*.
\]
Then
\[
R_0^t\prod_{i=1}^r\frac{\Gamma(t+\alpha_i)}{\Gamma(t+\delta_i)}
\]
satisfies the same functional equation as $F(\bbeta+t\bgamma\mid z_0)$.
It remains to identify these two functions of~$t$; this is a quite delicate part covered for most situations by \cite[Theorem~2.5]{BF22}. Note that the identification factor may also depend on~$t$.

An illustration given in \cite{BF22} deals with the case $(k,l,m)=(2,2,1)$ in which the vanishing of $Q_\bgamma(a+2t,b+2t,c+t,z)$ corresponds to that of
\begin{align*}
&
1 + a + b + a b - 2 c - a c - b c + c^2 + z + 2 a z + a^2 z + 2 b z +  a b z + b^2 z
\\ &\quad
- c z - a c z - b c z + (2 + a + b - 2 c + 7 z + 5 a z + 5 b z - 4 c z)t + (8z+1)t^2.
\end{align*}
The equations for the admissible quadruple are obtained by setting this polynomial in
$t$ identically zero; the corresponding system is solved by imposing
\[
z_0=-\tfrac18,\quad a=2t,\quad b=2t+\tfrac13,\quad c=t+\tfrac56
\]
or 
\[
z_0=-\tfrac18,\quad a=2t,\quad b=2t-\tfrac13,\quad c=t+\tfrac23.
\]
The first possibility leads to
\[
F\big(2(t+1),2(t+1)+\tfrac13,t+1+\tfrac56\mid -\tfrac18\big)
=\frac{16}{27}\times\frac{t+\tfrac56}{t+\tfrac23}\times F(2t,2t+\tfrac13,t+\tfrac56\mid -\tfrac18),
\]
while application of \cite[Corollary~2.8]{BF22} finally translates it into
\[
{}_2F_1\bigg(2t,2t+\frac13;t+\frac56 \Bigm| -\frac18\bigg)
=\bigg(\frac{16}{27}\bigg)^t\frac{\Gamma(t+\tfrac56)\Gamma(\tfrac23)}{\Gamma(t+\tfrac23)\Gamma(\tfrac56)}.
\]
A similar gamma evaluation is deduced for the second choice of admissible quadruple.

\section{Zeilberger's methodology}
\label{sec2}

There is another method to produce such closed-form evaluations.
It is similar in spirit and essentially equivalent to Ebisu's method discussed in Section~\ref{sec1}; it has been given by Zeilberger \cite{Ze05} a decade earlier.
A set of illustrative examples was provided by Shalosh B.~Ekhad in a separate piece \cite{Ek04}.
Zeilberger looks for a relation of the form
\begin{equation}\label{basic-Z}
F(\bbeta+(t+1)\bgamma\mid z)=\hat R_\bgamma(t,\bbeta,z)F(\bbeta+t\bgamma\mid z)+\hat Q_\bgamma(t,\bbeta,z)F(\bbeta+(t-1)\bgamma\mid z)
\end{equation}
instead of \eqref{functional}, then for conditions to eliminate the last term on the right-hand side and reduce the equality to
\begin{equation}\label{functional-Z}
F(\bbeta+(t+1)\bgamma\mid z_0)=\hat R_\bgamma(t,\bbeta,z_0) F(\bbeta+t\bgamma\mid z_0).
\end{equation}
Of course, at the end of the day the two functional relations \eqref{functional} and \eqref{functional-Z} tend out to be the same, so that solving for the vanishing of $\hat Q_\bgamma(t,\bbeta,z)$ is essentially the same task as doing this for $Q_\bgamma(\bbeta+t\bgamma,z)$.
There are some transparent differences though.

For Zeilberger's design \eqref{basic-Z} one does not need to know anything about contiguous relations: simply execute the Gosper--Zeilberger algorithm \cite{PWZ96} for the hypergeometric term
\begin{equation}\label{hyperterm}
A(t,n)=\frac{(a+kt)_n(b+lt)_n}{(c+mt)_n(1)_n}\,z^n
\end{equation}
to obtain the telescoping relation
\[
p_0(t)A(t+1,n)+p_1(t)A(t,n)+p_2(t)A(t-1,n)=B(t,n+1)-B(t,n)
\]
for some $B(t,n)$ which is a rational multiple of $A(t,n)$.
(The fact that the difference operator $p_0(t)T^2+p_1(t)T+p_2(t)$, with $T\colon t\mapsto t+1$ the shift operator, is of order at most~2 is guaranteed by the fact that $\sum_nA(t,n)$ is a $_2F_1$ hypergeometric series, in turn implied by the structure of contiguous relations discussed earlier.)
Summing over $n$ and checking the boundary behaviour of $B(t,n)$ at $n=0$ and $n=\infty$, leads to
\begin{equation}\label{basic-Z2}
p_0(t)F(\bbeta+(t+1)\bgamma\mid z)+p_1(t)F(\bbeta+t\bgamma\mid z)+p_2(t)F(\bbeta+(t-1)\bgamma\mid z)=0
\end{equation}
which is a form of \eqref{basic-Z}.
At the same time dealing with \eqref{basic-Z2} directly has its own advantages: for example, to reduce it to a shorter relation (that is, to a difference equation of order~1 as in \eqref{functional-Z}) we may look for either $p_0(t)=0$ or $p_2(t)=0$.
(These two strategies are essentially equivalent, as what comes out from executing one of them should be producible by the other.)
One can even look for $p_1(t)=0$; this leads to a first-order difference equation with respect to the shift $t\mapsto t+2$.
Furthermore, in most of the cases one can throw in an additional parameter $d$ into the hypergeometric term~\eqref{hyperterm}:
\begin{equation*}
%\label{hyperterm2}
A(t,n)=\frac{(a+kt)_n(b+lt)_n}{(c+mt)_n(d)_n}\,z^n
\end{equation*}
to still have the telescoping relation.
However, when $d\notin\mathbb Z_{>0}$, the difference equation in \eqref{basic-Z2} becomes in general inhomogeneous; solving it after reduction to order~1 requires extension of the results from~\cite{BF22}.

One more\,---\,purely technical\,---\,advantage of Zeilberger's scheme concerns finding appropriate $z_0$ for admissible quadruples. In both Ebisu's and Zeilberger's methods they come from the leading coefficients in the $t$ expansions of (the numerators of) the rational coefficients; in the form \eqref{basic-Z2} we just need the leading $t$-terms of $p_0(t)$ or $p_2(t)$ (in fact, of all three coefficients\,---\,this comes from a careful analysis of the hypergeometric structure).
The latter can be cheaply achieved for \emph{any} choice of $a,b,c$, so that we can first execute the algorithm of creative telescoping with the choice $a=b=c=0$ (well, we better take $c=1$ if $m$ coincides with either~$k$ or~$l$).
This leads to a shorter running time; after that we could run the algorithm again with $z_0$ specified but $a,b,c$ undetermined.

As a final remark, in spite of the obvious similarity of two methodologies, the webpage of \cite{Ek04} has the following addition on the 27th February 2014: ``Akihito Ebisu found many new amazing identities, using a novel new method'' and refers to what finally became \cite{Eb17}.

\section{WZ connections}
\label{sec3}

The fundamentals of the WZ machinery are well explained in the fundamental Wilf--Zeilberger paper \cite{WZ90}; the WZ acronym stands for the standard use of $w$ and $z$ as complex variables.
It is already made clear in \cite{Ze05} that an underlying mechanism behind gamma evaluations is via appropriate WZ pairs, that is, via hypergeometric terms $A(t,n)$ and $B(t,n)$ in two variables satisfying
\[
A(t+1,n)-A(t,n)=B(t,n+1)-B(t,n).
\]
In a general context of strange evaluations, Gessel \cite{Ge95} highlighted the importance of WZ-pairs already three decades ago.
This line has received a second birth in the recent work of Au \cite{Au24}, where he introduces a notion of WZ seed, with rules of generating infinitely many WZ pairs from a single one, and algorithmic strategies for realising a targetted identity in terms of a WZ seed.
The techniques from \cite{Au24} lead to proofs of numerous gamma evaluations which were open for years, in particular, of several Ramanujan-type formulas for (negative powers of) $\pi$;
these proofs in fact give multi-parameter extensions of such formulas for suitable choices of the differential parameter $z=z_0$, just like in Ebisu--Zeilberger evaluations but now for more general $_pF_{p-1}$ hypergeometric functions.
There is a limited supply for the choice of \emph{rational} $z_0$:%
\footnote{A heuristic explanation of what algebraic $z_0$ can show up does not exist at all.}
Gessel remarks in \cite[Sect.~9]{Ge95} about the 2-3-5 rule: one usually expects $z_0$ be admissible if both $z_0$ and $1-z_0$ involve the three smallest primes only in their factorisation (there are a few artificially designed exceptions though).
This is echoed in \cite{Au24} with a notice that even the prime $5$ does not originate from the WZ seeds coming from the classical hypergeometric summations.
Examples obtained in \cite{Ek04} or by the methods from \cite{Eb17,Ek04,Ze05} include gamma evaluations for
\[
{}_2F_1\big(-t,\tfrac12-t;\tfrac32+4t\mid\tfrac15\big), \quad
{}_2F_1\big(-t,\tfrac12-t;\tfrac52+4t\mid\tfrac15\big)
\]
and
\[
{}_2F_1\big(t,\tfrac12+t;6t\mid\tfrac45\big), \quad
{}_2F_1\big(t,\tfrac12+t;-1+6t\mid\tfrac45\big).
\]
Though they are weak as only depend on just one additional parameter~$t$, they can be extended to two-parameter (inhomogeneous!) gamma evaluations following a remark in Section~\ref{sec2}: each of the sums
\[
{}_3F_2\bigg(\begin{matrix} 1, \, -t, \, \tfrac12-t \\[2pt] d, \, 5d-\tfrac72+4t \end{matrix}\biggm|\frac15\bigg), \quad
{}_3F_2\bigg(\begin{matrix} 1, \, -t, \, \tfrac12-t \\[2pt] d, \, 5d-\tfrac52+4t \end{matrix}\biggm|\frac15\bigg)
\]
and
\[
{}_3F_2\bigg(\begin{matrix} 1, \, t, \, \tfrac12+t \\ d, \, 5-5d+6t \end{matrix}\biggm|\frac45\bigg), \quad
{}_3F_2\bigg(\begin{matrix} 1, \, t, \, \tfrac12+t \\ d, \, 4-5d+6t \end{matrix}\biggm|\frac45\bigg)
\]
solves a first order inhomogeneous difference equation (too lengthy though for displaying an example here).
Unlike the main results in \cite{BF22}, there is no general machinery to solve such inhomogeneous equations.
%So far no example with rational $z_0$ and corresponding to a gamma evaluation of $_2F_1$ or $_3F_2$ has been discovered.

\section{Higher rank reduction}
\label{sec4}

The two methods in \cite{Eb17} and \cite{Ze05} explore the same idea of forcedly reducing a rank~2 holonomic system to rank~1, using slightly different variants.
The work \cite{Eb17} furthermore outlines some possibilities for reducing higher-rank holonomic systems to rank~1, but not to rank 2 or higher (because of its design); this is discussed in \cite{Eb17} for $_3F_2$ (already known) evaluations and for Appell's $F_1$ double hypergeometric function.
Zeilberger's machinery can be extended to this setup along the lines.
In addition, one may source $_3F_2$ gamma evaluations from $_2F_1$ ones that match Clausen's formula
\[
{}_2F_1\big(a,b;a+b+\tfrac12\mid z\big)^2
={}_3F_2\bigg(\begin{matrix} 2a, \, 2b, \, a+b \\ 2a+2b, \, a+b+\tfrac12 \end{matrix}\biggm| z\bigg)
\]
or, more generally, Orr-type formulas \cite[Sect.~2.5]{Sl66}.
One example in \cite{BF22} corresponding to the shift $\bgamma=(-1,3,2)$ (see also \cite[p.~34, eq.~(ix)]{Eb17}) reads
\[
{}_2F_1\bigl(-t,3t+1,2t+\tfrac32\mid \tfrac14\bigr)
=\bigg(\frac{16}{27}\bigg)^t\frac{\Gamma(t+\frac54)\Gamma(t+\frac34)\Gamma(\frac76)\Gamma(\frac23)}{\Gamma(t+\frac76)\Gamma(t+\frac23)\Gamma(\frac54)\Gamma(\frac34)}
=\frac{2^{4t+2}\Gamma(2t+\frac32)\Gamma(\frac12)}{3^{3t+3/2}\Gamma(2t+\frac43)\Gamma(\frac23)};
\]
after Clausen-squaring it becomes
\begin{equation}
{}_3F_2\bigg(\begin{matrix} -2t, \, 6t+2, \, 2t+1 \\ 4t+2, \, 2t+\frac32 \end{matrix}\biggm| \frac14\bigg)
=\frac{2^{8t+4}\Gamma(2t+\frac32)^2\Gamma(\frac12)^2}{3^{6t+3}\Gamma(2t+\frac43)^2\Gamma(\frac23)^2}.
\label{Eb1}
\end{equation}
Similarly, the evaluation \cite[p.~36, eq.~(ix)]{Eb17}
\[
{}_2F_1\bigl(-t,3t+1;2t+\tfrac32\mid -\tfrac18\bigr)
=\frac{2^{3t+1}\Gamma(2t+\frac32)\Gamma(\frac12)}{3^{3t+1}\Gamma(t+\frac76)\Gamma(t+\frac56)}
\]
leads to
\begin{equation*}
{}_3F_2\bigg(\begin{matrix} -2t, \, 6t+2, \, 2t+1 \\ 4t+2, \, 2t+\frac32 \end{matrix}\biggm| -\frac18\bigg)
=\frac{2^{6t+2}\Gamma(2t+\frac32)^2\Gamma(\frac12)^2}{3^{6t+2}\Gamma(t+\frac76)^2\Gamma(t+\frac56)^2}.
%\label{Eb2}
\end{equation*}

Zeilberger's method \cite{Ze05} allows one to deal with a more general sum $a(t)=F(\bbeta+t\bgamma\mid z)$,
when $\bbeta$ and $\gamma$ correspond to the $_pF_{p-1}$ hypergeometric function parameters.
The corresponding difference equation
\[
\sum_{i=0}^rp_i(t)a(t+i)=0
\]
of order $r\le p$ can be further reduced to a lower order when $p_r(t)=0$ (or $p_0(t)=0$) via an appropriate choice of the parameters. This does not (explicitly) rely on contiguous relations and give, for example, reductions of rank~3 holonomic systems to rank~2; the bottleneck is the running time.
Applying this method to some $_3F_2$-series (for which running time is finite) we found that
\[
{}_3F_2\bigg(\begin{matrix} \frac13, \, t, \, -\frac13+2t \\ \frac23, \, \frac12+t \end{matrix}\biggm| 2\bigg),
% (2^k Pochhammer[1/3, k] Pochhammer[t, k] Pochhammer[-(1/3) + 2 t, k])/(k! Pochhammer[2/3, k] Pochhammer[1/2 + t, k])
\quad
{}_3F_2\bigg(\begin{matrix} \frac23, \, t, \, -\frac23+2t \\ \frac43, \, \frac12+t \end{matrix}\biggm| 2\bigg),
% (2^k Pochhammer[2/3, k] Pochhammer[t, k] Pochhammer[-(2/3) + 2 t, k])/(k! Pochhammer[4/3, k] Pochhammer[1/2 + t, k])
\quad
{}_3F_2\bigg(\begin{matrix} \frac12, \, t, \, 1-t \\ 1, \, \frac12+t \end{matrix}\biggm| \frac14\bigg)
\]
satisfy second rather than third order difference equations in~$t$.
For example, if we denote the latter hypergeometric function by $G(t)$ then
\[
t(4t-1)(4t+1)G(t+1) - (2t+1)(10t^2-10t+3)G(t) + (t-1)(2t-1)(2t+1)G(t-1)=0.
\]
At $t=\frac12$, the series possesses the closed form
\begin{equation*}
{}_3F_2\bigg(\begin{matrix} \frac12, \, \frac12, \, \frac12 \\ 1, \, 1 \end{matrix}\biggm| \frac14\bigg)
=\frac{\sqrt3\,\Gamma(\frac13)^6}{2^{8/3}\pi^4}
%\label{Eb1s}
\end{equation*}
which is a special case, when $t=-\frac14$, of the evaluation~\eqref{Eb1}.

\section{$q$-Extensions}
\label{sec5}

There seems to be no straightforward way to extend the methodology from \cite{Ze05} and \cite{Eb17} to a $q$-setting;
as the examples below indicate the $q$-extensions rarely found for $_2F_1$ gamma evaluations come from a system of holonomic rank higher than~$2$, so their reduction to rank~$1$ is hardly explainable.
However such $q$-analogues of formulas from \cite{Eb17} do exist, and they are provable using classical basic hypergeometric techniques \cite{GR04} and creative telescoping \cite{PWZ96} or $q$-WZ pairs \cite{WZ90}.

Chern's identity \cite{Ch23}
\begin{equation}
\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(q^2/a;q^2)_k(a;q)_k}{(q^3;q^3)_k(a^2q;q^2)_k}(-1)^kq^{\binom{k+1}2}a^k
=\frac{(aq;q^2)_\infty(a^3q^3;q^6)_\infty}{(a^2q;q^2)_\infty(q^3;q^6)_\infty}
\label{eq:id1}
\end{equation}
is one of such instances, which played a crucial role in the recent resolution of a combinatorial conjecture of Andrews and Uncu.
The identity can be proved by showing that the summand
\[
F_k(a,q)=\frac{(q^2/a;q^2)_k(a;q)_k}{(q^3;q^3)_k(a^2q;q^2)_k}(-1)^kq^{\binom{k+1}2}a^k
\]
satisfies the telescoping relation
\[
(1-a^2q)(1-a^6q^3)F_k(aq,q)-(1-a^4q)(1-a^4q^3)F_k(a,q)=G_{k+1}(a,q)-G_k(a,q)
\]
for a suitable choice of $G_k(a,q)$.

A similar strategy works for
\begin{equation}
\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(q/a,a^2;q)_k}{(q^3,a^3q^2;q^3)_k}\,(1+aq^{2k})\,q^{k^2}a^k
=\frac{(-a;q)_\infty(a^2q;q^2)_\infty(q^2;q^3)_\infty}{(a^3q^2;q^3)_\infty}.
\label{eq:id2}
\end{equation}

Identity \eqref{eq:id1} is a $q$-analogue of Ebisu's formula \cite[p.~27, Sect.~4.3.3, eq.~(xiv)]{Eb17},
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(1-a)_k(2a)_k}{k!\,(2a+\frac12)_k}\,\biggl(-\frac13\biggr)^k
=\frac{\Gamma(\frac12)\Gamma(2a+\frac12)}{3^a\Gamma(a+\frac12)^2},
\]
while identity \eqref{eq:id2} is a $q$-analogue of \cite[p.~27, eq.~(A.18)]{Eb17} (see also \cite[p.~696]{BF22}),
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(1-a)_k(2a)_k}{k!\,(a+\frac23)_k}\,\biggl(\frac19\biggr)^k
=\frac{3^a\Gamma(\frac12)\Gamma(a+\frac23)}{4^a\Gamma(\frac23)\Gamma(a+\frac12)}.
\]

As L.~Wang points out, identity \eqref{eq:id1} is a specialisation of \cite[Exercise 3.29(i)]{GR04} (see also \cite[Corollary 6]{CW09}): write it as
\begin{align}
&
\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(1-cq^{5k})(q^2/a,c;q^2)_k(a;q)_k(cq/a^2;q^3)_k(acq;q^6)_k}{(1-c)(q^3,acq;q^3)_k(a^2q;q^2)_k(cq^2/a,cq^4/a;q^4)_k}(-1)^kq^{\binom{k+1}2}a^k
\nonumber\\ &\quad
=\frac{(cq^2,aq;q^2)_\infty(cq^4/a^2,a^3q^3;q^6)_\infty}{(cq^2/a,a^2q;q^2)_\infty(q^3,acq^4;q^6)_\infty}
\label{eq:id3}
\end{align}
(notice the correction of typo in the product side) and choose $c=0$.
Now \cite[Exercises 3.29(ii), (iii)]{GR04} do not seem to possess suitable specialisations ($c=0$ is boring, and the series diverge as $a\to0$).
They suggest however the existence of a shifted version of \eqref{eq:id3} (which, unfortunately, does not follow from \cite[Proposition~5]{CW09}).

Specialisation $a=0$ of \cite[Corollary 10]{CW09} (or the shift $b\mapsto b/q^3$ in \cite[Corollary~9]{CW09}) reads
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(q;q^2)_k(b;q^4)_k}{(q^4;q^4)_k(bq^3;q^6)_k}(-1)^kq^{k^2+2k}
=\frac{(b;q^4)_\infty(q^3;q^6)_\infty(q^{12};q^{12})_\infty}{(q^4;q^4)_\infty(bq^3;q^6)_\infty(b;q^{12})_\infty};
%\label{eq:id4}
\end{equation*}
this is a $q$-analogue of Ebisu's \cite[p.~26, eq.~(x)]{Eb17}.

Specialisation $a=0$ and $m\to\infty$ of \cite[Section~3.1, the first display]{CC21} leads to
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(b,q/b;q)_k}{(q^2;q^2)_k(qd;q)_k}q^{\binom{k+1}2}d^k
=\frac{(qbd,q^2b/d;q^2)_\infty}{(qd;q)_\infty};
%\label{eq:id5}
\end{equation*}
this is a $q$-analogue of \cite[p.~22, eq.~(vii)]{Eb17}.

Specialisation $a=0$ of Rahman's \cite[eq.~(1.8)]{Ra93} results in
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(b,d;q)_k}{(q;q)_k(qbd;q^2)_k}q^{\binom{k+1}2}
=\frac{(qb,qd;q^2)_\infty}{(q,qbd;q)_\infty}.
%\label{eq:id6}
\end{equation*}

Some other $q$-analogues of $_2F_1$ gamma evaluations can be found or extracted from the existing literature;
they however do not suggest a general method.
Perhaps, linking the corresponding $_2F_1$ hypergeometric sums with WZ pairs, connecting the latter with the classical WZ seeds from \cite{Au24} and performing the $q$-deformation of the latter as explained in Au's further work \cite{Au24b} will give one an algorithmic way of finding $q$-extensions.

\section{An attempt to conclude}
\label{sec6}

There are other techniques in use, somewhat algorithmic as well, to produce non-standard gamma evaluations of hypergeometric functions, for example, those discussed in \cite{CS13,GS82,Go81}.
Strange evaluations resulting from both Ebisu's and Zeilberger's methods automatically depend on an  an additional parameter~$t$. This limits their supply considerably. 
There is no evidence that the evaluations
\begin{align*}
{}_3F_2\biggl(\begin{matrix} \frac12, \, \frac12, \, \frac12 \\ 1, \, 1 \end{matrix} \biggm|\frac1{64}\biggr)
&=\frac{2}{7\pi}\prod_{j=1}^{7}\Gamma\biggl(\frac j7\biggr)^{\left(\frac j7\right)}
\\ \intertext{(this is the original example of CM-evaluation from \cite[\S\,8]{SC67}) and}
{}_3F_2\biggl(\begin{matrix} \frac12, \, \frac16, \, \frac56 \\ 1, \, 1 \end{matrix} \biggm|-\frac1{80^3}\biggr)
&=\frac{4\sqrt{15}}{43\pi}\prod_{j=1}^{42}\Gamma\biggl(\frac j{43}\biggr)^{\left(\frac j{43}\right)},
\end{align*}
where $\big(\frac{\cdot}{N}\big)$ denotes the Legendre symbol, possess $t$-parametric extensions.
Is there a method to prove such rigid identities?

title: Theory of Mind in Action: The Instruction Inference Task
summary:
The Theory of Mind (ToM) refers to an agent's capacity to infer the mental
states of other agents. ToM is essential for effective collaboration. To assess
ToM in a dynamic, goal-oriented, and collaborative environment, we introduce a
novel task, Instruction Inference, in which an agent assists a principal in
reaching a goal by interpreting indirect or ambiguous instructions. We present
Tomcat, an LLM-based agent, designed to exhibit ToM reasoning in interpreting
and responding to the principal's instructions. We implement two variants of
Tomcat. One, dubbed Fs-CoT, is based on a small number of examples (i.e.,
few-shot or Fs) demonstrating the requisite structured reasoning (i.e.,
chain-of-thought or CoT). One, dubbed CP, relies on commonsense knowledge and
information about the problem (i.e., commonsense prompt or CP). We realized
both variants of Tomcat on three leading large language models (LLMs), namely,
GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, and Gemma-3-27B. To evaluate the effectiveness of Tomcat,
we conducted a study with 52 human participants in which we provided
participants with the same information as the CP variant of Tomcat. We computed
intent accuracy, action optimality, and planning optimality to measure the ToM
capabilities of Tomcat and our study participants. We found that Tomcat with
Fs-CoT, particularly with GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1, achieves performance
comparable to the human participants, underscoring its ToM potential for
human-AI collaboration.

title: PathGene: Benchmarking Driver Gene Mutations and Exon Prediction Using Multicenter Lung Cancer Histopathology Image Dataset
summary:

assessment. Faced with regional disparities in medical resources and the high

\begin{abstract}
  Accurately predicting gene mutations, mutation subtypes and their exons in lung cancer is critical for personalized treatment planning and prognostic assessment. Faced with regional disparities in medical resources and the high cost of genomic assays, using artificial intelligence to infer these mutations and exon variants from routine histopathology images could greatly facilitate precision therapy. Although some prior studies have shown that deep learning can accelerate the prediction of key gene mutations from lung cancer pathology slides, their performance remains suboptimal and has so far been limited mainly to early screening tasks. To address these limitations, we have assembled PathGene, which comprises histopathology images paired with next-generation sequencing reports from 1,576 patients at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University, and 448 TCGA-LUAD patients. This multi-center dataset links whole-slide images to driver gene mutation status, mutation subtypes, exon, and tumor mutational burden (TMB) status, with the goal of leveraging pathology images to predict mutations, subtypes, exon locations, and TMB for early genetic screening and to advance precision oncology. Unlike existing datasets, we provide molecular-level information related to histopathology images in PathGene to facilitate the development of biomarker prediction models. We benchmarked 11 multiple-instance learning methods on PathGene for mutation, subtype, exon, and TMB prediction tasks. These experimental methods provide valuable alternatives for early genetic screening of lung cancer patients and assisting clinicians to quickly develop personalized precision targeted treatment plans for patients. Code and data are available at \url{https://github.com/panliangrui/NIPS2025/}.
 % and \url{https://huggingface.co/datasets/LiangruiPan/PathGene-CSU_svs} 
\end{abstract}


\section{Introduction}
Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, accounting for over 1.8 million deaths annually. Despite advances in targeted therapies and immunotherapies, the five-year overall survival rate for advanced non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains below 25\% \cite{kratzer2024lung},\cite{hanna2017systemic}. Precise identification of driver gene mutations (e.g., TP53, EGFR, KRAS, ALK), their specific subtypes and exon locations, and rapid, cost-effective prediction of tumor mutational burden (TMB) are critical for effective treatment stratification and personalized therapy \cite{wu2018management}, \cite{kris2014using}, \cite{goodman2017tumor}. Conventional molecular testing methods, such as next-generation sequencing (NGS) or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays, are the reference standard for mutation detection and TMB assessment. However, they require invasive biopsies, may be limited by tissue availability, and are time-consuming, labor-intensive, and costly \cite{coudray2018classification}. These constraints disproportionately burden low-resource regions and economically disadvantaged patients, impeding equitable access to genomic testing.


In lung cancer development, driver genes confer a selective growth advantage by activating oncogenic signaling pathways and sustaining clonal tumor expansion, thereby driving tumor initiation, progression, invasion, and therapy resistance \cite{weinstein2013cancer,hanahan2011hallmarks}. As critical biomarkers for precision targeted therapies, these genes determine the observable phenotypic features in histopathology images \cite{imielinski2012mapping}. Conversely, histopathology slides can be analyzed to infer the mutational status of lung cancer driver genes \cite{rios2017somatic}. However, traditional histopathological analysis, relying on the experience and judgment of pathologists, cannot directly reveal mutation information at the genetic level. With advances in computational pathology, digitized whole-slide images (WSIs) now provide standardized, high-resolution input data for artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms \cite{qu2021genetic}. WSIs offer a wealth of information related to tumor growth and progression, which encompassing cellular-level, tissue-level, and tumor-heterogeneity features. By analyzing these data, one can visually infer alterations in lung cancer driver genes, thereby advancing the development of precision oncology. \cite{unger2024deep}.

Recent studies have shown that deep learning can directly infer genomic variants from digitized hematoxylin and eosin tumor histopathology images \cite{coudray2018classification},\cite{fu2020pan},\cite{fidon2024histology}. This approach leverages routinely acquired slides to provide a non-destructive, one-stop solution that reduces turnaround time and increases accessibility in resource-limited settings. Initial studies using convolutional neural networks achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) values above 0.75 for specific driver mutations such as EGFR and KRAS \cite{coudray2018classification}, \cite{lu2021ai}. Subsequent multiple instance learning (MIL) algorithms have been widely applied to gene-mutation prediction tasks \cite{qu2021genetic,sundaram2018predicting,acosta2022intratumoral,zhao2025deep}, and more recently, Transformer-based models have attracted substantial interest \cite{xu2024whole,wang2024pathology,xiang2025vision}. However, most existing work has focused on single-gene or partial-gene predictions and has not addressed driver-mutation subtypes, exon variants, or TMB. These biomarkers (mutation subtypes and exon alterations) can markedly change protein structure and function, informing targeted-drug development, while TMB predicts tumor immunogenicity and response to immunotherapy \cite{sattler2025expanding,niknafs2023persistent}. Additionally, many studies based on a single cohort raises general concerns about the generalizability of the models.%are restricted to single-institution cohorts, raising concerns about generalizability across diverse patient populations and imaging protocols.

To address these gaps, we assembled a large, multicenter cohort of digitized WSIs linked to matched driver-gene sequencing data and constructed the PathGene dataset (see Figure~\ref{figure1}(a)). PathGene is designed to enable WSI-based prediction of (1) driver-gene mutation status (TP53, EGFR, KRAS, ALK), (2) detailed TP53 mutation subtypes, (3) categories of exons in mutation-driven genes, and (4) TMB status. To evaluate the efficacy and generalizability of MIL methods for lung-cancer driver-gene prediction, we benchmarked 11 state-of-the-art models on these four tasks and examined their potential for precision oncology. The MIL models trained based on PathGene can first assist in the early screening of gene mutations in lung cancer patients. Secondly, for patients with confirmed driver gene mutations, the subtypes and exons of their driver genes can be obtained, and then NGS testing of some genes can be performed to analyze the targeted drugs that patients can benefit from. Clinical analysis indicates that 65\% of patients could avoid unnecessary full-panel NGS testing, reducing both cost and turnaround time. Our results offer important insights into the clinical utility of AI in precision medicine and underscore the real-world impact of pathology-driven molecular prediction. In summary, our contributions are as follows:

\begin{enumerate}
	\item \textbf{Multicenter Lung Cancer Histopathology Image Dataset:} PathGene comprises digitized WSIs from 1,576 lung cancer patients at Xiangya Second Hospital (PathGene-CSU) and 448 LUAD patients from The Cancer Genome Atlas(TCGA) (PathGene-TCGA\_LUAD). We provide the original WSIs (available upon request) and the feature embeddings of the WSIs.
	\item \textbf{Multicenter Lung Cancer Driver-Gene Dataset:} We matched the genetic testing data for all 2,024 patients in PathGene, and collated and provided information on driver gene mutations, gene mutation subtypes, exons, and TMB status of lung cancer patients.
	\item \textbf{Extensive Benchmarks:} We conducted a comprehensive benchmark test on four tasks, namely gene mutation, gene mutation subtype, exon and TMB status, using 11 MIL methods based on the PathGene dataset, and verified the potential of AI in predicting lung cancer driver genes and TMB status.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related work}

%\subsection{Gene pathology dataset}
Previous research has primarily focused on interpreting histopathology images for cancer diagnosis, using datasets annotated with tumor subtype, survival outcomes, pathology reports, or immunohistochemistry markers \cite{cancer2014comprehensive,coudray2018classification,chen2025whole}. These labels aid diagnosis but cannot identify which patients will benefit from immunotherapy. TCGA was among the first large public resources to link WSIs with whole-exome sequencing data (including mutation annotations and TMB for classic driver genes), covering more than 11,000 samples from 33 cancer types (e.g., LUAD, LUSC), thereby enabling numerous AI-based prediction efforts \cite{cancer2014comprehensive}. The Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) built on TCGA by adding proteomic profiles, yielding multimodal cohorts (e.g., LUAD, ovarian cancer) that facilitate investigation of relationships between morphology, genotype, and proteomics and cross-center validation of mutation-prediction models \cite{li2023proteogenomic}. The Human Tumor Atlas Network (HTAN) further contributes high-quality, multicenter multi-omic (genomic, transcriptomic, spatial-omic) and WSI data, supporting fine-grained mutation localization and microenvironment analyses. However, TCGA and CPTAC suffer from limited gene-tested cohort sizes, uneven sample quality, and class imbalance, while HTAN lacks large-scale, exon-level mutation annotations across multiple driver genes \cite{rozenblatt2020human}. To address the limited availability of NGS data in lung cancer patients, we constructed the PathGene-CSU dataset, comprising 1,576 patients with matched WSIs and genetic testing results. This dataset provides comprehensive annotations of driver gene mutation status, mutation subtypes, exon-level variations, and TMB. In addition, we curated the PathGene-TCGA\_LUAD dataset. Together, the PathGene datasets enable systematic benchmarking of AI models for mutation discovery and facilitate the development of early screening strategies and personalized treatment plans for targeted therapies.

\section{PathGene dataset}


\subsection{Dataset collection}
In this retrospective study, we trained and validated baseline models using anonymized WSIs from two cohorts: a local cohort at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University (PathGene-CSU), and the TCGA\_LUAD (PathGene-TCGA\_LUAD) cohort. We included only WSIs from patients who met all of the following criteria: (1) a histopathologic diagnosis of LUAD or tumors containing adenocarcinoma components; (2) availability of NGS-based driver-gene testing reports; (3) inclusion of both tumor and adjacent non-tumor tissue in routine sections; and (4) high slide quality (no folding, wrinkling, blurring, or color artifacts). An experienced pathologist identified patient IDs with NGS reports in the medical records and retrieved the corresponding WSIs from the archive. From April 2020 to December 2023, 38,706 patients underwent lung nodule resection at the Second Xiangya Hospital, of whom 1,930 had clear NGS reports; after quality control, 1,576 WSIs and their matched clinical data comprised PathGene-CSU. We applied the same inclusion criteria to select histopathology images and genetic data for the PathGene-TCGA\_LUAD cohort.



\subsection{Dataset organization}

\textbf{PathGene‐CSU:} The PathGene‐CSU cohort comprises 1,576 lung cancer patients, predominantly diagnosed with adenocarcinoma or adenosquamous carcinoma. All patients underwent NGS, yielding per‐patient labels for driver‐gene mutation status, mutation subtypes, and exon‐level variant locations. We focus on five prediction tasks: (1) binary mutation status (0/1) for TP53, EGFR, KRAS, and ALK; (2) TP53 mutation subtype (wild‐type, nonsense, missense); (3) TP53 exon hotspots (EX5, EX6, EX7, EX8, other) based on functional‐domain distribution \cite{baugh2018there,yu2021tp53}; (4) EGFR exon (EX19, EX20, EX21), chosen for their mutation frequency, TKI sensitivity, and clinical response differences \cite{yasuda2013structural,sequist2011genotypic}; and (5) binary TMB status (high/low; 9 mut/Mb cutoff). For KRAS, we consolidate EX3 and rarer exons into an “other” category due to low sample counts. ALK subtypes are divided into EML4–ALK fusions and non‐fusion point mutations, reflecting the availability of fusion‐targeted therapies. %Please see Appendix (\textbf{A.2}) for the relevant detailed classification standards.

\textbf{PathGene‐TCGA‐LUAD:} This dataset includes 510 WSIs from 448 TCGA\_LUAD patients. Multiple WSI from the same tumor share identical NGS report. We retrieved driver‐gene labels from cBioPortal and define mutation status as 0/1 and TMB status (high/low) at a 10 mut/Mb threshold \cite{sha2020tumor}. TP53 subtypes were reclassified by pathologists as wild-type/nonsense mutation/missense mutation. Due to the limited and uniform nature of the exons for the target gene mutations (296, 75, 29, and 48 exons, respectively), the experiment was unable to predict these mutations at the exon level in this dataset.
 %Exon‐level prediction was not evaluated here owing to insufficient per‐exon sample sizes (total counts: 296, 75, 29, 48).


\subsection{Data preprocessing}

WSI is saved in svs format based on a 20$\times$ magnification. As shown in Figure~\ref{figure1}(b), we first use the Otsu algorithm to distinguish the background area of the WSI, and use the sliding window strategy to divide the WSI into $256 \times 256$ pixel patches based on the field of view under a 20$\times$ magnification, and mark the spatial position of the patches \cite{otsu1975threshold}. For patch feature extraction, we use CTransPath to extract one-dimensional features from each patch to enrich the diverse feature representation of WSI \cite{wang2022transformer}. CTransPath is based on the Swin Transformer architecture and consists of three convolutional layers and four Swin Transformer modules \cite{liu2021swin}. It can extract local features from image data and capture global features and long-range dependencies. Based on CTransPath, the embedded features of the patches are extracted, and each patch embedding is unified into a 768-dimensional vector representation. Therefore, all patches at each scale in the WSI are represented as feature vectors $V$. However, the patches in the WSI have spatial position relationships, and we use the K nearest neighbor (KNN) algorithm (K=9) to construct the nodes and edges of the spatial topology graph ($G$) \cite{keller1985fuzzy,chen2020pathomic}. Therefore, the feature representation of each WSI is $G = (V,E)$.

\subsection{Dataset splits}

In all downstream tasks related to driver gene prediction, we employ five-fold cross-validation to evaluate baseline model performance. Specifically, the dataset is partitioned into five subsets; in each iteration, four subsets are used for training while the remaining one is used for validation. This process is repeated five times, and the average performance across all folds is reported to estimate the model’s generalizability. Compared to leave-one-out cross-validation, five-fold cross-validation makes more efficient use of the data and reduces evaluation bias introduced by random partitioning.

\section{Evaluation and benchmarks}

Our objective is to develop and validate MIL models that utilize histopathology images to accurately predict multiple key biomarkers, thereby advancing early cancer screening and personalized treatment. We propose four complementary prediction tasks: (1) mutation status of driver genes, for early detection and risk stratification; (2) mutation subtypes of driver genes, to facilitate molecular classification; (3) specific exons of mutated driver genes, to optimize targeted therapy strategies; and (4) TMB classification (high vs. low), to assess potential responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibitors. This benchmark is designed to evaluate whether MIL models can automatically learn and extract morphological features from standard WSIs that are strongly associated with these biomarkers, thereby providing interpretable, non-invasive support for clinical decision-making. Furthermore, it promotes the advancement of key technologies such as weakly supervised learning, explainable AI, and multi-scale feature fusion.

\subsection{Experimental setup}
\subsubsection{Task definition}

\textbf{Gene mutation prediction:} The task of predicting mutant genes using histopathological images aims to predict whether a driver gene has mutated by building a deep learning-based image analysis model to extract tissue morphological features related to gene mutation status from digital pathological sections. This task is usually formulated as a binary classification problem, where the model takes the features of WSIs ($x \in {R^{n \times 768}}$) as input and outputs the mutation status label ($y \in \{ 0,1\} $) of the driver gene. That is, learn a model ${f_\theta }:x \to \hat y$ parameterized by $\theta $, such that $\hat y \approx y$.

\textbf{Gene mutation subtype prediction:} The task of predicting mutant gene subtypes using histopathological images aims to build a prediction model that can automatically identify gene mutation types or subtype states from digital pathological sections. This task is a multi-classification task, and the input is the features of WSIs, which can be represented as $x \in {R^{n \times 768}}$. A categorical label $y \in \{ 1,...,K\}$ indicating the mutation subtype of a driver gene, where $K$ may include classes such as wild-type, missense, nonsense. The goal is to learn a model ${f_\theta }:x \to \hat y$ that minimizes the multi-class cross-entropy.

\textbf{Exon prediction:} The task of predicting mutant gene exons using histopathological images aims to mine morphological features related to gene mutation status from digital pathological images of tissue sections through computational methods such as deep learning, and then infer the mutation status at the exon level of a specific gene. The definition of this task is similar to that of the gene mutation subtype task.

\textbf{TMB Status Prediction:} This task focuses on predicting TMB status using histopathological images. MIL models are trained on WSIs and classified the tested WSI into high or low TMB status. This task is usually defined as a binary classification problem, similar to the gene mutation prediction task.

\subsubsection{Baselines methods}

To evaluate the performance of our PathGene benchmark, we selected a suite of state-of-the-art models based on MIL. Given the rich pathological information embedded in WSIs, we employed various single-scale MIL methods, including ABMIL \cite{ilse2018attention}, CLAM \cite{lu2021data}, DSMIL \cite{li2021dual}, TransMIL \cite{shao2021transmil}, DTFD-MIL \cite{zhang2022dtfd}, IBMIL \cite{lin2023interventional}, HIPT \cite{chen2022scaling}, MHIM \cite{tang2023multiple}, R2T\_MIL \cite{tang2023multiple}, and Patch-GCN \cite{chen2021whole}, to conduct comprehensive evaluations across four tasks. These models represent significant advancements in MIL and have demonstrated high predictive potential in multiple histopathological image datasets. For detailed methodological information and implementation, please refer to the appendix.


%\subsubsection{Experiment Environment}



\subsubsection{Evaluation metrics}

In the experiment, we used AUROC, Accuracy (ACC), Precision, Recall, and F1-Score values as evaluation indicators for the model’s performance in predicting gene mutations, mutation subtypes, and exons \cite{flach2015precision,chen2020classification}. The larger the AUROC, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-Score values, the better. All evaluation metrics were reported as the mean and standard deviation (std) across five-fold cross-validation to assess model performance.


\subsection{Results}
\textbf{Prediction of gene mutation:} We conducted a large number of comparative experiments on the PathGene-CSU and PathGene-TCGA\_LUAD datasets and summarized the results in Table~\ref{gene_mutation-CSU} and Table~\ref{gene_mutation-LUAD}. TransMIL consistently outperformed other models due to its self-attention-based cross-patch association modeling capabilities. Specifically, on the PathGene-CSU dataset, the AUROC values for TP53, EGFR, KRAS, and ALK mutations were approximately 0.9215, 0.9044, 0.8843, and 0.9121, respectively. On the PathGene-TCGA\_LUAD dataset, the corresponding AUROCs also exceeded 0.84, with KRAS achieving a notable 0.963. These results underscore the effectiveness of the Transformer architecture in capturing subtle morphological and microenvironmental changes associated with driver gene mutations. In contrast, the CLAM-SB and the CLAM-MB both demonstrated strong performance across most tasks, particularly in identifying KRAS and ALK mutations, achieving results very close to those of TransMIL. This suggests that incorporating clustering constraints or multi-view attention mechanisms within a MIL framework enhances model efficacy. Conversely, models relying solely on single-patch attention or static graph structures, such as ABMIL, IBMIL, and Patch-GCN, generally lagged by 10\% to 20\%. This performance gap indicates that local features or static topologies are insufficient for comprehensively capturing the molecular phenotype information present in WSIs. Therefore, effective pathological image-genome mapping necessitates integrating both global associations and local details. However, the results achieved by RRT\_MIL and MHIM have not yet reached clinical-grade performance, and their model architectures may require continuous optimization. \textbf{Prediction of gene mutation subtypes:} To explore the potential of MIL models in predicting TP53 mutation subtypes, we conducted large-scale experiments using 11 MIL methods on the PathGene dataset, and summarized their AUROC values along with other metrics in Table~\ref{TP53-CSU} and Table~\ref{TP53-LUAD}. In the PathGene-CSU, TransMIL demonstrated the strongest overall performance, achieving an average AUROC of 0.8684 and an average accuracy of 0.7772. It also led on average precision, recall, and F1-score (0.8362). Both CLAM-MB and CLAM-SB performed consistently well, with AUROCs near 0.863 and F1-scores above 0.75, underscoring the value of attention-based MIL for capturing mutation-related morphological features. By contrast, traditional MIL methods such as ABMIL (AUROC 0.5997) and DSMIL (AUROC 0.5958) underperformed markedly, indicating the limitations of relying solely on instance-level representations and local attention. Although Patch-GCN incorporates graph-based spatial modeling, its F1-score of 0.5936 remains inferior to Transformer-based approaches, suggesting challenges in fully integrating tissue spatial context. On the PathGene-TCGA\_LUAD dataset, both TransMIL and RRT-MIL excelled: TransMIL achieved an average AUROC of 0.8996 and RRT-MIL attained 0.8995, with average F1-scores of 0.8513 and 0.8484, respectively. Their strong global-patch modeling underpins robust transferability and generalization. In contrast, the CLAM models’ F1-scores dropped by approximately 20\%, revealing sensitivity to distribution shifts and image heterogeneity. Likewise, methods such as IBMIL, HIPT, and MHIM exhibited pronounced declines in accuracy and precision, reflecting overfitting and weak feature generalization in small-sample or cross-institutional contexts.

\textbf{Exon prediction:} Given the limited number of driver gene mutations in TCGA\_LUAD, which results in fewer and imbalanced exon labels, we evaluated the performance of 11 MIL models for predicting driver gene exons of lung cancer mutations only on the PathGene-CSU dataset. The AUROC values and other evaluation metrics are summarized in appendix (Table~\ref{exon-CSU}, Table~\ref{TP53-exon}, Table~\ref{EGFR-exon}, Table~\ref{KRAS-exon} and Table~\ref{ALK-exon}). TransMIL achieved the highest performance for TP53 and EGFR prediction, with average AUROCs of 0.9004 and 0.8694 and accuracies of 0.818 and 0.8218, respectively (Table~\ref{TP53-exon}, Table~\ref{EGFR-exon}). This result underscores TransMIL’s strong capacity to capture morphology-based mutation signals in high-resolution pathology images. CLAM-SB and CLAM-MB also performed robustly on TP53 and KRAS, each attaining AUROCs near 0.90, demonstrating their generalizability across complex histopathological data. Conversely, MHIM and RRT\_MIL underperformed across all genes (AUROCs below 0.60 and low accuracies; Table~\ref{TP53-exon}, Table~\ref{EGFR-exon}), revealing significant bottlenecks in their architectures for this task. These findings highlight that architectural design and training strategies critically influence the extraction of molecularly relevant features from pathology images. Future work should therefore prioritize optimizing network structures and data augmentation strategies to enhance the accuracy and reliability of gene‐mutation prediction in digital histopathology. Furthermore, we found a substantial disparity between precision and recall in exon-level KRAS predictions, which may stem from the highly imbalanced distribution of exon labels (with exon 2 accounting for 85\% to 98\% of all KRAS mutation labels). However, this label imbalance is intrinsic to the underlying gene mutation pattern itself.

\textbf{TMB status prediction:} To validate the ability of MIL models to predict TMB status from WSIs, we evaluated the performance of 11 MIL models on the PathGene-CSU dataset, with the results summarized in Table~\ref{TMB-CSU} and Table~\ref{TMB-LUAD}. In a systematic evaluation on the PathGene‐CSU and PathGene‐TCGA\_LUAD datasets, TransMIL demonstrated the most consistent and superior performance among multiple MIL models. It achieved the highest (or near-highest) AUROCs of 0.911 ± 0.0796 on PathGene‐CSU and 0.9076 ± 0.0819 on PathGene‐TCGA\_LUAD, along with F1-scores of 0.9208 ± 0.0708 and 0.9183 ± 0.0639, respectively. TransMIL also led across accuracy, precision, and recall, underscoring its robustness and generalizability in capturing discriminative features related to TMB from WSI. CLAM-SB and CLAM-MB likewise exhibited strong results, particularly on the PathGene-CSU dataset, where each model approached 0.96 accuracy and precision and exceeded 0.89 in F1-score—evidence of their capacity to fit specific data distributions. In contrast, traditional approaches such as MHIM and RRT\_MIL fell short, with AUROCs below 0.55. Although these models occasionally registered higher precision, their markedly lower F1-scores reveal limitations in modeling complex histopathological patterns. Overall, this comparison highlights the advantage of Transformer-based architectures for WSI-level gene mutation prediction and confirms that sophisticated attention mechanisms and global context modeling are critical to enhancing both generalization and predictive accuracy.

\section{Limitation}
Recent deep learning approaches have advanced the prediction of gene mutations from histopathological images; however, several limitations persist. Firstly, dataset-related challenges include difficulties in standardizing tissue preparation, quality control, and digitization processes, leading to variability in image quality. Additionally, the high cost of NGS hampers large-scale testing of lung cancer patients, particularly in resource-limited settings. Secondly, analysis of driver gene mutations reveals that certain mutations predominantly occur within specific exons. For instance, approximately 65\% of KRAS mutations are localized to a single exon, resulting in inherent label imbalance within datasets. Expanding the collection of NGS data could mitigate this imbalance. Model-related limitations are also evident. Not all gene mutations manifest discernible morphological changes in histopathological images, making it challenging for models to detect such alterations based solely on visual features. The association between genetic mutations and histological patterns is often indirect, mediated by intermediate molecular mechanisms such as alterations in gene expression or signaling pathways. Furthermore, class imbalance in mutation frequencies (where common mutations dominate and rare mutations are underrepresented) may bias the predictive performance of the model. The interpretability of deep learning models remains a critical concern; it is frequently unclear which morphological features correspond to specific genetic alterations, thereby limiting clinical trust and applicability. Tumor heterogeneity and sampling bias further complicate molecular characterization, as different tissue regions may exhibit varying genetic profiles, potentially compromising prediction reliability. Lastly, relying solely on histopathological images for gene mutation prediction represents a unimodal approach. Integrating multimodal data (radiological imaging, genomic profiles, and clinical records) could enhance model performance and interpretability. Addressing these challenges necessitates the collection of high-quality, multimodal datasets and the development of more robust, interpretable models to improve biomarker prediction in lung cancer.


\section{Conclusion and future work}


This paper introduces PathGene, the largest, most comprehensive, and multi-center lung cancer histopathology WSI dataset to date, which includes matched driver gene sequencing reports. PathGene-CSU comprises 1,576 lung cancer patients from the Second Xiangya Hospital of Central South University, making it the largest open-access WSI collection with corresponding NGS data. Unlike existing histopathology image datasets, PathGene-CSU includes detailed annotations for key driver genes, enabling MIL models to perform noninvasive early genetic screening and to identify patients likely to benefit from targeted or immune therapies. We further constructed PathGene-TCGA\_LUAD by linking TCGA\_LUAD WSIs to their molecular profiles. Through extensive baseline experiments on these cohorts, we demonstrate that MIL models accurately predict driver-gene mutation status, triage patients for focused NGS testing, and achieve strong performance on mutation-subtype and exon-level prediction (despite label imbalance). Moreover, our models can distinguish high versus low TMB. These results underscore the potential of AI-driven image analysis to advance precision oncology and guide personalized treatment strategies for lung cancer.

\subsection{PathGene collection}
We assembled a cohort of 1,576 patients with lung cancer who underwent NGS according to predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, thereby establishing the PathGene‐CSU dataset. In the WHO Classification of Lung Cancer released in 2021, the detection of predictive biomarkers was listed as a "desirable standard", but are not incorporated into the formal disease nomenclature system. This means that, unless in specific circumstances, the WHO does not mandate genetic testing for lung squamous cell carcinoma. The molecular testing guidelines jointly issued by the CAP, IASLC, and the AMP state \cite{cancer2014comprehensive}, \cite{steels2001role}: "In resected specimens of lung cancer, EGFR and ALK testing is recommended for adenocarcinomas and mixed-type lung cancers with adenocarcinoma components. For lung cancers lacking any adenocarcinoma component, such as pure squamous cell carcinoma, pure small cell carcinoma, or undifferentiated carcinoma without any immunohistochemical evidence, EGFR and ALK testing is not recommended." Furthermore, both the 2013 and 2018 guidelines explicitly state \cite{cancer2014comprehensive}, \cite{steels2001role}: "For pure squamous cell carcinoma, routine molecular testing for EGFR and ALK is not recommended." Consequently, clinical practice rarely generates NGS reports for squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, and our PathGene‐CSU collection comprises 1,576 lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) patients and only 10 lung adenosquamous carcinomas (LUAC). Finally, we compiled patients’ clinical baselines from PathGene‐CSU and PathGene‐TCGA\_LUAD NGS reports, as detailed in Table~\ref{baseline}.

\subsection{PathGene organization}
%In this study, pathologists have reclassified the subtypes of TP53 mutations into three categories: wild-type, nonsense mutations, and missense mutations. In lung cancer, the TP53 wild-type gene, also known as wild-type TP53 (Wtp53), performs functions including promoting tumor cell apoptosis, preventing cell transformation, and stabilizing the genome. These actions inhibit the generation and transformation of tumor cells, promote tumor cell apoptosis, and protect the body from tumor cell invasion during tumorigenesis and development \cite{yang2020hsp90}. In lung cancer, TP53 nonsense mutations refer to a type of point mutation in the TP53 gene, resulting in a premature stop codon during mRNA translation. This leads to a truncated p53 protein that loses its normal function \cite{cancer2014comprehensive}, \cite{steels2001role}. Such nonsense mutations are relatively common in lung cancer and are closely associated with tumor invasiveness, treatment resistance, and poor prognosis. In lung cancer, TP53 missense mutations refer to point mutations that replace one amino acid with another in the p53 protein encoded by TP53, altering the protein's structure and function. These mutations often result in the loss of normal tumor-suppressing functions of the p53 protein and may sometimes acquire new oncogenic functions (gain-of-function), thereby accelerating cancer cell proliferation and enhancing invasiveness \cite{cancer2014comprehensive}, \cite{steels2001role}. This experiment focuses solely on predicting the subtypes of TP53.
%Exons are parts of eukaryotic genes that can be translated into corresponding amino acids. The human genome contains approximately 180,000 exons (about 30 megabases), accounting for about 1\% of the human genome. The complete set of exons is referred to as the exome \cite{ng2009targeted}, \cite{ng2010exome}. Exome sequencing typically involves first using targeted enrichment techniques to capture the exonic regions of the genome, followed by high-throughput sequencing to obtain the coding sequences, thereby identifying genetic features associated with diseases. Based on the biological relevance of TP53 mutations, we have categorized them into exon-specific categories (e.g., EX5, EX6, EX7, EX8) \cite{baugh2018there}, [8]. Exons 5–8 encode the DNA-binding domain (DBD), and data from COSMIC and TCGA confirm that over 75\% of TP53 mutations in lung adenocarcinoma occur in these regions. These exons contain pathogenic hotspot mutations (e.g., R175, G245, R248, R273), which differ functionally and clinically from mutations in other regions [9]. In lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), EGFR gene mutations are primarily concentrated in exons 19 (EX19), 20 (EX20), and 21 (EX21) [10]. This classification is based on mutation frequency, sensitivity to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), and differences in clinical treatment responses [11]. Furthermore, we have grouped KRAS mutations by exon (e.g., EX2, EX3) based on the biological and clinical significance of known mutation hotspots. EX2 (codons 12/13) accounts for over 90\% of all KRAS mutations in LUAD, particularly the G12C mutation, which has direct therapeutic implications [12]. EX3 includes the Q61 mutations, which affect GTPase activity and may represent a distinct molecular subgroup [13]. Other exons rarely contain mutations with clear clinical relevance. ELM4-ALK is the most frequent fusion type of ALK. Our genetic testing data indicate that most ALK mutations are ELM4-ALK fusions, along with other partner fusions (e.g., KIF5B, KLC1, PTPN3, STRN), point mutations, and amplification mutations (collectively referred to as “other” in Figure 3c).

Exome sequencing typically uses targeted enrichment to capture exonic regions followed by high-throughput sequencing to identify coding variants. Based on the biological relevance of TP53 mutations, we categorized them into exon-specific groups (EX5–EX8). Exons 5–8 encode the DNA‐binding domain (DBD), and data from COSMIC and TCGA confirm that over 75\% of TP53 mutations in lung adenocarcinoma occur in these regions, which harbor hotspot residues such as R175, G245, R248, and R273. In LUAD, EGFR mutations cluster in exons 19, 20, and 21 (EX19, EX20, EX21), reflecting mutation frequency, TKI sensitivity, and distinct clinical responses. KRAS mutations were grouped by exon: EX2 (codons 12/13) accounts for over 90\% of KRAS mutations in LUAD (notably G12C) with direct therapeutic implications, while EX3 (codon Q61) mutations affecting GTPase activity define a separate molecular subgroup. Other exons harbor mutations of limited clinical relevance. The EML4–ALK fusion is the predominant ALK alteration; other partners (KIF5B, KLC1, PTPN3, STRN), point mutations, and amplifications are collectively designated "other".

\subsubsection{TMB calculation criteria}
Gene Sequencing Company applied the following four criteria to select mutations for TMB calculation:
\begin{enumerate}
	\item Exclude variants with low sequencing depth (\(<500\times\) for tissue gDNA, \(<200\times\) for WBC gDNA) or poor quality (mapping quality \(<30\), base quality \(<30\)); remove variants with fewer than 2 reads in WBC gDNA.
	\item Exclude variants with allele frequency \(\ge30\%\) in WBC DNA as germline, except frameshifting indels or truncating SNVs in any of 15 canonical clonal hematopoiesis genes.
	\item Retain nonsynonymous SNVs/indels ($\pm 2\,\mathrm{bp}$ from splice sites) in coding regions.
	\item Remove variants present in >1\% of samples in dbSNP, 1000 Genomes, ESP6500, ExAC, or an in‐house database.
\end{enumerate}
High-confidence somatic mutations remaining after filtering were used for TMB. For tissue TMB, variants with $\mathrm{AF}<3\%$ were excluded. TMB was calculated as:
\[
\mathrm{TMB}
= \frac%
{\text{Number of high-confidence somatic mutations}}%
{\text{Panel-covered genomic length (Mb)}}%
\]

Using the upper‐quartile method and a lung cancer cutoff of $9\,\text{mut}/\text{Mb}$, samples were classified as TMB‐Low (TMB-L) or TMB-High (TMB-H).

\section{Experiment}

\subsection{Experimental setup}
We implemented our models in PyTorch 2.3 on a Linux server equipped with four NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs (24 GB each), 256 GB of DDR4 RAM, and dual Intel Xeon Gold CPUs. Data preprocessing and visualization leveraged OpenSlide (v3.4.1) for WSI loading, GAN-based augmentation for image
enhancement, and standard libraries, including NumPy (v1.23.5), pandas (v1.5.3), and scikit-learn (v1.2.2). During training, we utilized CUDA Toolkit 11.7, cuDNN 8.5, and NVIDIA’s Apex mixed-precision library to accelerate computation and optimize GPU memory usage. All networks were trained for 100 epochs using the Adam optimizer (learning rate = 0.001, $\beta_1$ = 0.9, weight decay = 0.9) with a batch size of one. The batch size of one accommodates the variable number of patches per WSI and the resulting graphs’ differing adjacency matrix sizes, which preclude uniform size batching.


\subsection{Baseline models}
\textbf{ABMIL} is an attention mechanism-based deep multiple instance learning method, primarily designed to handle bag-level classification tasks (e.g., Tumor malignancy grade in histopathological images), while preserving the ability to interpretably locate key instances. Its core framework is implemented in three stages: first, a neural network maps instances within a bag into low-dimensional embedded features; next, these instance features are aggregated in a permutation-invariant manner using dynamic attention weights combined with a gating mechanism; finally, label prediction is performed based on the aggregated bag embeddings. Compared to traditional methods, ABMIL achieves a balance between performance and efficiency through end-to-end training. %It has demonstrated superior performance on datasets such as MNIST-BAGS, breast cancer, and colon cancer, particularly excelling in few-shot learning scenarios. Additionally, ABMIL can intuitively locate the critical instances (e.g., lesion areas in pathological images) that trigger the bag-level label through attention weights, fulfilling legal requirements for model interpretability in the medical domain.

\textbf{CLAM-SB} (Single-Branch Model) is a simplified variant of the CLAM (Clustering-constrained-attention multiple-instance learning) framework specifically designed for binary classification tasks, such as distinguishing between tumor and normal tissue. The model identifies diagnostically significant sub-regions through a single attention module, treating regions with high attention scores as evidence for the positive class, while simultaneously using attention maps from other categories as supervisory signals to enforce cluster constraints. For example, in lymph node metastasis detection, CLAM-SB automatically focuses on micro-metastatic regions and optimizes the feature space via an instance-level clustering loss, encouraging a clear separation between positive and negative samples. Its main advantage lies in its lightweight architecture, making it well-suited for scenarios with limited data and mutually exclusive classes.

\textbf{CLAM-MB} (Multi-Branch Model) is designed for multi-subtype classification tasks such as differentiating subtypes of renal cell carcinoma or non-small cell lung cancer and employs a parallel attention branch architecture. Each branch corresponds to a specific class, independently computing class-specific attention weights and generating slide-level feature representations. For instance, in the classification of renal cell carcinoma, the three branches of CLAM-MB are dedicated to clear cell carcinoma, papillary carcinoma, and chromophobe carcinoma, respectively. A competitive attention mechanism is used to select key morphological features for each subtype, such as cytoplasmic clearing or papillary structures. Additionally, cross-branch clustering constraints are introduced to enforce feature-space separation among high-attention regions of different subtypes, thereby improving classification specificity and interpretability.

\textbf{DSMIL} (Dual-Stream Multiple Instance Learning Network) is a weakly supervised deep learning model designed for WSI classification. Its key innovations include a dual-stream aggregation architecture, self-supervised feature learning, and a multi-scale feature fusion mechanism. In DSMIL, a WSI is treated as a bag containing multiple instances (image patches), and the model is trained using only slide-level labels. To enhance feature representation, DSMIL employs a self-supervised contrastive learning strategy based on the SimCLR framework to pretrain the feature extractor. This allows the model to learn robust patch-level representations without the need for local annotations, while also reducing memory consumption when handling large bags. Furthermore, the model incorporates a pyramid-style multi-scale fusion approach that concatenates features extracted from image patches at different magnification levels. This design preserves global tissue architecture while capturing detailed cellular morphology across scales. Additionally, by sharing low-level features across scales, DSMIL imposes spatial continuity constraints on attention weights, which improves both classification accuracy and the precision of lesion localization.

\textbf{TransMIL} is a Transformer‐based correlated multiple instance learning framework tailored for weakly supervised WSI classification. It formally introduces the “correlated MIL” paradigm and provides a convergence proof, thereby overcoming the traditional MIL assumption of instance independence by explicitly modeling inter‐instance correlations via self‐attention. Architecturally, TransMIL employs ResNet50 to extract feature embeddings from WSI patches, which are then concatenated into a sequence for Transformer processing. Two parallel attention modules are incorporated to separately capture morphological and spatial information from the patches. A Pyramid Position Encoding Generator (PPEG) is devised to encode each patch’s two‐dimensional coordinates at multiple scales, with PPEG layers interposed between and following the Transformer encoder blocks to reinforce spatial dependency modeling. Before Transformer application, the patch sequence undergoes a “squaring” operation and a CLS token is prepended for global aggregation, allowing the resulting pooling matrix to contain both diagonal self‐attention weights and off‐diagonal cross‐instance correlation weights. The CLS token’s output is fed into a simple fully connected classification head to yield a bag‐level prediction, ensuring both training efficiency and high interpretability. 


\textbf{DTFD-MIL} addresses the paucity of WSIs by virtually expanding each slide into multiple pseudo bags, each inheriting the parent slide’s label. In Tier 1, an attention-based MIL model is trained on these pseudo-bags to produce initial bag-level predictions and to derive instance-level probabilities via Grad-CAM under the AB-MIL framework. However, since some pseudo-bags from positive slides may contain no true positives, Tier 2 distills representative feature vectors from each pseudo bag, using strategies like selecting the top-scoring instance (MaxS) or both top and bottom (MaxMinS) and retrains a second attention-based MIL model on the original slide bags, effectively correcting mislabeled pseudo-bags and enhancing robustness. This two-stage distillation cascade yields more discriminative slide-level embeddings, producing substantial accuracy gains over single-tier MIL on CAMELYON-16 and TCGA lung cancer cohorts while maintaining strong generalization across datasets.

\textbf{IBMIL} reframes WSI classification as a causal inference task by treating the bag‐level contextual prior as a confounder that induces spurious correlations between slide‐level labels and instance embeddings. To approximate distinct context strata, IBMIL first learns bag‐level feature representations via the conventional two‐stage MIL pipeline. First comes the feature extractor,followed by the aggregator. A "confounder dictionary" is then built by clustering these packet features using $K$ means. During the interventional training phase, IBMIL applies a backdoor adjustment strategy that reweights the influence of each context cluster through a learned attention mechanism over the confounder dictionary. Crucially, this intervention module is orthogonal to the choice of feature extractor and aggregation network, allowing IBMIL to be seamlessly integrated into and improved upon any existing MIL framework.

\textbf{HIPT} is a two-stage, multi-scale MIL framework that models WSIs via a coarse-to-fine pyramid of patch resolutions. In the first stage, the slide is partitioned into large, low-resolution tiles whose embeddings are processed by a Transformer encoder to capture global tissue architecture. The resulting “coarse” CLS representations are then distilled down to guide the second stage, where smaller, high-resolution tiles are encoded by a separate Transformer; here, the coarse CLS tokens act as teachers, enforcing consistency via a distillation loss so that fine-scale features remain aware of the overall context. To fuse spatial hierarchy, HIPT employs overlapping windowed self-attention and incorporates positional encodings that respect both tile location and pyramid level. This hierarchical distillation not only accelerates convergence by allowing the coarse model to provide robust initialization for the fine model but also yields richer, multi-scale slide embeddings that improve classification accuracy and interpretability, particularly in low-data or highly heterogeneous pathology cohorts.

\textbf{MHIM} streamlines attention-based MIL by explicitly mining “hard” instances to improve robustness. A momentum “teacher” model scores patches, identifying those of intermediate difficulty, while a “student” model is trained on masked subsets that include both easy and hard examples. The teacher’s weights update via exponential moving average of the student, guiding the student to focus on diagnostically challenging patches. This mask-based instance reweighting yields more balanced learning, reduces overfitting, and consistently outperforms standard MIL baselines on WSI classification tasks.

\textbf{RRT\_MIL} augments any backbone–aggregator pipeline by re-embedding patch features on-the-fly through a lightweight Transformer module. After extracting block embeddings (e.g., using ResNet-50), it partitions them into local regions and applies small Transformers (with relative or convolutional positional encodings) to refine these embeddings before MIL aggregation. During training, regions (1D or 2D blocks) are ranked by their refined scores and reweighted: top regions receive higher attention while lower-ranked ones are downplayed. This plug-and-play R²T block enables end-to-end fine-tuning of both the backbone and MIL head, yielding large AUROC gains across CAMELYON-16, TCGA-NSCLC, and other cohorts compared to static-feature MIL methods.


\textbf{Patch-GCN} treats a WSI as a 2D point cloud where each patch becomes a graph node and edges connect spatially adjacent patches via k-nearest neighbors, explicitly encoding tissue architecture and local context for downstream tasks.  Patch features are first extracted with a CNN backbone (e.g., ResNet-50) and serve as initial node embeddings for a multi-layer graph convolutional network (GCN) that performs message passing to aggregate both morphological characteristics and neighborhood interactions. To capture multi-scale structures, a hierarchical clustering strategy groups patches globally and locally to form subgraphs that preserve macroscopic distribution patterns as well as microscopic histological details, and these subgraphs are processed sequentially or in parallel by GCNs.  After GCN layers, a slide-level representation is obtained via a global readout operation (mean, max, or attention pooling), which is then fed into a classifier or survival-prediction head.

\subsection{Discussion on pathology foundation models and expert models}
Although the aforementioned Foundation models demonstrate the capability to predict pathological images across institutions, their predictive accuracy remains suboptimal. Our evaluation of these models on genetic testing tasks reveals that expert models significantly outperform them, as detailed in Table~\ref{big}. Furthermore, existing literature highlights that the quality of histopathological images is influenced by various factors, including discrepancies in sample processing and preparation, variations in digital scanning equipment and parameters, differences in standardization and quality control measures, and the experience and technical proficiency of personnel. These factors collectively impact the generalizability of the models. Notably, discussions in the Prov-GigaPath study published in Nature emphasize that predicting gene mutations poses greater challenges, potentially due to the insufficiency of single-scale pathological image information in capturing certain alterations. Therefore, we advocate for the standardization of film preparation, scanning procedures, and quality control measures as a prerequisite for cross-center testing of histopathological images, facilitating more robust cross-center validation.

\section{Ethical review}
This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. This study was a retrospective analysis of digital images of anonymized archived tissue samples from nine patient cohorts. The collection and anonymization of patients in all cohorts was performed at each contributing center. The research use of all external independent cohorts was approved by each participating center. The experiments were all performed using lung cancer tissue samples from the Second Xiangya Hospital of Central South University and were approved by the Ethics Committee of the Second Xiangya Hospital of Central South University (Ethics Review Document Z0161-01).

title: BlastDiffusion: A Latent Diffusion Model for Generating Synthetic Embryo Images to Address Data Scarcity in In Vitro Fertilization
summary:
Accurately identifying oocytes that progress to the blastocyst stage is
crucial in reproductive medicine, but the limited availability of annotated
high-quality embryo images presents challenges for developing automated
diagnostic tools. To address this, we propose BlastDiffusion, a generative
model based on Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) that synthesizes realistic oocyte
images conditioned on developmental outcomes. Our approach utilizes a
pretrained Variational Autoencoder (VAE) for latent space representation,
combined with a diffusion process to generate images that distinguish between
oocytes that reach the blastocyst stage and those that do not. When compared to
Blastocyst-GAN, a GAN-based model we trained for this task, BlastDiffusion
achieves superior performance, with a global Frechet Inception Distance (FID)
of 94.32, significantly better than Blastocyst-GAN's FID of 232.73.
Additionally, our model shows improvements in perceptual (LPIPS) and structural
(SSIM) similarity to real oocyte images. Qualitative analysis further
demonstrates that BlastDiffusion captures key morphological differences linked
to developmental outcomes. These results highlight the potential of diffusion
models in reproductive medicine, offering an effective tool for data
augmentation and automated embryo assessment.
